explanations: luna: The source-section root ر ب ب appears in رَبَّكُمُ; the command to worship your Lord is grounded in His having created the people and those before them. | terra: “Worship your Lord” (ٱعْبُدُوا۟ رَبَّكُمُ) immediately identifies Him as the one who created people, joining Rabb, createdness, and service.
luna: God commands the angels to prostrate to Adam; the honored human receives obeisance while remaining a creature under God's command, matching the section's honored-servant secondary sense.
luna: Pharaoh's people slaughtered sons and spared women; this earlier telling supplies the oppression behind the enslavement scene.
terra: The required cow is لَّا ذَلُولٌ for ploughing or watering the field, a deliberate negative boundary for the tamed animal sense of muzallal.
luna: The covenant commands Israel to worship none but Allah; this is a binding statement of the exclusive service voiced in 1:5.
luna: The source-section root م ل ك appears in مُّلْكُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ; sovereignty belongs to God alone, and no protector or helper exists besides Him.
luna: What is in the heavens and earth belongs to Allah, and all are devoutly obedient to Him; possession and service appear together.
luna: Jacob asks his sons whom they will worship after him; their answer names the one God of their fathers, presenting service as the creature's inherited allegiance.
terra: “Innā lillāhi wa innā ilayhi rājiʿūn” puts belonging to God and return to Him in the servants’ own voice.
luna: Righteousness includes giving wealth to free those in bondage, فِي الرِّقَابِ; the verse makes release a direct reversal of the owned-slave scene.
terra: When “My servants” ask about God, He answers that He is near and responds to their call, supplying the direct reciprocal relation behind a servant’s appeal for help.
luna: The verse describes a person selling himself to seek God's approval, a specific self-surrender parallel to the section's servant accepting his belonging.
luna: The verse says a believing slave woman is better than a polytheist woman, even if the latter attracts the listener; faith, not free status, determines the relevant worth.

luna: The source-section's root م ل ك is widened by مَالِكَ الْمُلْكِ: God grants and removes human dominion, showing that human ownership is received and bounded. | terra: مَٰلِكَ ٱلْمُلْكِ gives and removes rule and both honors and abases; ownership here actively determines the high and low position developed by the image.

luna: Jesus says Allah is his Lord and the people's Lord, then commands them to worship Him; the human messenger remains a servant under the same Lord. | terra: Jesus says, “God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him,” a direct human voice refusing the Lord role while enjoining service.

luna: The source-section root ر ب ب appears in أَرْبَابًا; the call says not to take one another as lords apart from Allah, setting a boundary on human beings occupying the Lord's place. | terra: The call refuses taking one another as أَرْبَابًا besides God, directly limiting the human master relation the section traces in Rabb.

luna: The source-section root ر ب ب appears in رَبَّانِيِّينَ, while the verse denies that a prophet would tell people to become his servants instead of God's; human teaching authority cannot claim worship. | terra: A recipient of revelation may not tell people, “be عِبَادًا لِّى”; even elevated human authority cannot turn people into its own servants.

luna: The source-section root ر ب ب appears in أَرْبَابًا; the verse explicitly says prophets and angels must not be taken as lords, marking the limit of human mastery. | terra: The revelation-bearer cannot command people to take angels or prophets as arbāb; this continues 3:79’s boundary against creatures claiming lordship.

luna: The verse says all in the heavens and earth submit to Allah willingly or unwillingly and return to Him, expressing the created servitude behind 19:93. | terra: All in heaven and earth submit to God willingly or unwillingly under His دِين, making the created servant’s belonging antecedent to a chosen verbal confession.

luna: The verse speaks of believing slave women under one's right hand and requires permission and a dowry for marriage; it treats the owned person as a party with rights. | terra: Marriage with believing slave women and “some of you are from others” makes legal slave status coexist with shared human and religious standing.

luna: The source-section root ع ب د appears in the command to worship Allah alone; the same verse then names those under one's right hand, joining exclusive divine service to the owner's responsibility toward dependents. | terra: The command to worship God includes doing good to those whom the right hand possesses, holding human ownership under worship and ethical care.
luna: The verse commands obedience to God, the Messenger, and those in authority, but sends disputes back to God and the Messenger; human authority remains bounded.
luna: Whoever obeys the Messenger obeys Allah; this makes human obedience derivative rather than an independent lordship.
luna: The expiation for accidental killing includes freeing a believing slave, تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ مُّؤْمِنَةٍ; an owned person is released as part of repairing harm.
luna: The source-section root م ل ك appears in لِلَّهِ مَا فِى السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ, and root ع ب د in عَبْدًا لِلَّهِ; all belong to Allah and the Messiah is not too proud to serve Him.

luna: The verse says the Messiah does not disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor do the angels near Him; it makes honored rank compatible with servanthood. | terra: The Messiah and near angels do not disdain being عَبْدًا لِّلَّهِ: exalted rank does not cancel creaturely servanthood.
luna: The continuation contrasts believers who receive their full reward with those too proud to serve; it completes 4:172's claim about refusing servitude.

luna: Jesus's statement that Allah is his Lord and theirs is paired with “worship Him”; it makes the worshipper's relation to the Lord explicit. | terra: The Messiah commands worship of God as his and their Lord, while the verse warns against associating partners; it fixes the boundary between honored messenger and worshipped Lord.
luna: Among the expiations for a broken oath is freeing a slave; this is another specific reversal of the section's human-as-property scene.
terra: God questions Jesus about making him and his mother two gods; the scene rejects turning honored human servants into objects of worship.
terra: Jesus says his sole command was “worship God, my Lord and your Lord,” completing 5:116 by returning worship to the shared Rabb.
luna: Whatever is in the heavens and earth belongs to Allah, then He joins that ownership to gathering everyone on the Day of Judgment; all lesser property is under the true Owner.
luna: God is the creator and the one who feeds but is not fed; this marks the provider as master and the dependent creature as recipient.
terra: God is ٱلْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ, placing the owner above the abd without the need or lowliness denied in 17:111.
terra: Again He is al-Qahhār above His servants, now in the scene of guardians and death, so ownership reaches the servants’ final return.
luna: The verse says dominion belongs to Him when the trumpet is blown; it joins the source-section's ملك root to the final accounting.

luna: The source-section root ر ب ب appears in رَبُّكُمْ and root ع ب د in فَاعْبُدُوهُ; Allah is Lord and creator of everything, grounding the command to serve Him. | terra: God is Creator of everything and is therefore to be worshipped (فَٱعْبُدُوهُ); creation is stated as the warrant for service.
luna: The Lord is rich in mercy and can remove people and replace them; this shows that the owner depends on no human servants.
luna: The speaker gives prayer, sacrifice, life, and death to Allah, Lord of the worlds; the verse expands servant allegiance across the whole life.
luna: The verse recalls humanity's creation and God's command to the angels to prostrate to Adam; it repeats the specific honor given to a created servant.
luna: Iblis refuses the prostration and claims superiority over Adam; the continuation contrasts commanded service with pride.
luna: Noah tells his people to worship Allah alone and fear the account of a tremendous day, making the servant's duty answerable to God.
luna: Hud gives his people the same direct call to worship Allah alone; it repeats the exclusive Lord-servant relation in another community.
luna: Salih's call to worship Allah alone is paired with a sign from their Lord, placing the people's duty under the one who provides the sign.
luna: Shuayb commands worship of Allah alone and fair measure; the verse joins service to the Lord with limits on human handling of goods.
luna: Pharaoh's response to his chiefs includes slaughtering sons and sparing women; it continues the same human domination that Moses calls enslavement in 26:22.
terra: The rescue from Pharaoh’s house, with its degrading violence against Israel, supplies the oppression behind Moses’s word abbadta in 26:22.
terra: At the covenant God asks, “Am I not your رَبّ?” and they answer yes; it stages the creature’s own acknowledgment of the Lord relation later voiced in worship.
luna: The source-section root ع ب د appears in عِبَادٌ أَمْثَالُكُمْ; those invoked besides Allah are servants like the people invoking them, so the supposed lords are themselves creatures.
terra: Those with your Lord do not grow too proud for His worship, but glorify and prostrate; the abd’s lowliness is enacted without degrading God.

luna: The source-section root ر ب ب appears in أَرْبَابًا; the verse says some took rabbis, monks, and the Messiah as lords besides Allah, showing the human religious mastery distinguished from God's. | terra: Taking rabbis and monks as أَرْبَابًا shows the forbidden transfer of lordly obedience to human religious authorities.
luna: One use of alms is emancipation, وَفِي الرِّقَابِ; the verse directs wealth toward freeing people held in bondage.
luna: God says He has purchased the believers' lives and wealth in exchange for Paradise; this gives a chosen covenantal form to the section's relation of owner and owned.
luna: The source-section root ر ب ب appears in رَبُّكُمْ; after naming Allah as Lord and creator, the verse says فَاعْبُدُوهُ, connecting divine ownership with worship.
terra: God asks who possesses hearing and sight, brings living from dead and dead from living, and governs the affair, making malik-like possession effective over faculties and life.
luna: The speaker says he is commanded to worship Allah, not those invoked besides Him; it states the boundary between the true Lord and rival objects of service.
luna: The warning says to worship none but Allah; it is a direct formulation of the exclusive service in the section's central address.
luna: Hud tells his people to worship Allah, their only deity; this repeats the human community's obligation to its Lord.
luna: The source-section root ر ب ب appears in إِنَّ رَبِّى and root ع ب د in the opening command; Salih links Allah's bringing people from earth and settling them there to their service.
luna: Shuayb again commands worship of Allah alone while forbidding short measure and weight, tying exclusive service to the conduct of owners and traders.

luna: The source-section's root ر ب ب in its human-master sense appears in إِنَّهُ رَبِّي within Yusuf's household. The section's reading fits the householder, while the wording can also be heard as “my Lord.” | terra: In the master’s house Yusuf calls the one who gave him good lodging رَبِّى, preserving the source’s concrete human sense of Rabb as master of a dwelling.
terra: The pair find her سَيِّدَهَا at the door, materially locating the master-and-household scene invoked in 12:23.
terra: The wife of the Aziz is said to solicit her fatā, adding the household’s owned young servant to the master-house scene of 12:23–25.

luna: The source-section root ر ب ب appears in أَرْبَابٌ مُّتَفَرِّقُونَ; Yusuf asks whether separate lords are better than Allah, the One and Prevailing, directly testing human masters against the true Lord. | terra: Yusuf asks whether many separate أَرْبَابٌ are better than God the One, the Compeller, setting competing human-style masters against the sole true owner.

luna: The source-section roots ع ب د and د ي ن meet: the verse commands worship of Allah alone, إِلَّا إِيَّاهُ, and calls this الدِّينُ الْقَيِّمُ, matching the section's account of din as obedience and servitude. | terra: Yusuf joins “only Him worship” with ٱلدِّينُ ٱلْقَيِّمُ in one command, closely matching iyyāka naʿbudu and dīn.

luna: The source-section's root ر ب ب in the human-master sense appears when a prisoner is to serve wine to his رَبِّ (master); the term applies to a human owner. | terra: Yusuf says one prisoner will serve wine to his رَبّ, a plain human-master use of the same word the section reads in Rabb.

luna: Yusuf asks to be remembered with the prisoner's رَبِّ (master, the king); this neighbour repeats the human use of the source-section's root ر ب ب. | terra: “Mention me to your rabb” uses rabb for the freed prisoner’s earthly master, distinguishing this household vocabulary from divine lordship.

luna: Yusuf tells the released messenger to return to his رَبِّ (master, the king); this continues the Qur'anic human-master use of ر ب ب. | terra: The king tells the messenger to return to his rabb; this is another concrete human authority carried by Rabb.
terra: Yusuf could not keep his brother under the dīn of the king, showing dīn as the binding rule or jurisdiction of a ruler as well as religious obedience.
luna: All in the heavens and earth prostrate to Allah willingly or unwillingly, and their shadows do too; this gives a bodily image of creation's subjection.
luna: Moses reminds Israel that Pharaoh's people inflicted terrible torment, slaughtered sons, and spared women; the ayah recalls the human subjection behind the section's slave image.
luna: After God fashions the human and breathes into him of His spirit, He commands the angels to prostrate; this supplies the created-human context for the honor scene.
luna: The angels all prostrate in response to the command; this continues the specific act of honoring Adam.
luna: Iblis alone refuses; the passage makes prideful refusal the reversal of obedient service.
terra: Satan has no authority over God’s servants except followers who go astray, drawing a boundary around which master may command them.
luna: Livestock provide warmth, benefits, and food; the verse presents the material goods in the master's scene as gifts made available by God.
luna: The herd is beautiful as people drive it out to pasture and bring it home, a specific domestic livestock scene.
luna: The animals carry burdens to distant lands that people could not reach without hardship, matching the section's useful, domesticated animal.

luna: Horses, mules, and donkeys are named for riding and adornment, directly matching the horse among the master's possessions. | terra: Horses, mules, and donkeys are created for riding and adornment, supplying the image’s owned horse with its Qur’anic creaturely source.
luna: Those invoked besides Allah have created nothing and are themselves created; the verse reverses the relation by identifying the alleged masters as made things.
luna: The next ayah says those invoked are dead, not living, and do not know when they will be raised; it completes the contrast with the living Creator.

luna: Every community receives a messenger calling it to worship Allah and avoid the ṭāghūt; this makes the Lord-servant relation universal and distinguishes rightful service from submission to a false master. | terra: Every community receives the command to worship God and avoid tāghūt, framing worship as a choice between the true master and coercive rivals.
luna: All creatures in the heavens and earth prostrate to Allah; the verse pictures creation's bodily submission rather than only naming it.
luna: The next ayah says the angels fear their Lord above them and do what they are commanded; it completes the prostration scene with obedience.
terra: Everything in heaven and earth belongs to God, and “to Him is the dīn always” (وَلَهُ ٱلدِّينُ وَاصِبًا), explicitly binding universal possession to enduring allegiance.
terra: The bee is told to travel the paths of its Lord as ذُلُلًا, bringing the section’s made-easy/tamed road together with a working creature.

luna: The source-section root م ل ك appears in مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُهُمْ; the verse contrasts favored owners with those under their hands and asks why they will not share alike. | terra: Those given more provision do not make what their hands possess equal sharers in it; the human ownership scene is used to reject equals being assigned to God.

luna: The source-section roots ع ب د and م ل ك meet in عَبْدًا مَّمْلُوكًا لَّا يَقْدِرُ عَلَىٰ شَىْءٍ; the comparison with the provided spender clarifies what ownership and capacity mean. | terra: The parable explicitly stages عَبْدًا مَّمْلُوكًا unable to do anything against a person given good provision who spends it; it is the section’s owned-slave and providing-owner scene.

terra: The dependent, speechless man is a burden on his مَوْلَاهُ, unlike one who commands justice; the comparison keeps the master-dependent relation concrete while refusing to make it a divine equality.
terra: God takes His عَبْدِهِ by night on an honored journey, a narrative in which the named servant is distinguished and cared for.
terra: “Your Rabb has decreed that you worship none but Him” directly binds the Lord-title to exclusive obedience.
luna: The verse repeats God's command that the angels prostrate to Adam and records Iblis's refusal, another direct formulation of the human honor scene.
terra: God repeats that Satan has no authority over “My servants,” then names the Lord sufficient as guardian, adding protection to divine possession.

luna: The source section's secondary dictionary sense describes the muʿabbed as honored and exalted; this verse says the children of Adam were honored, while the section keeps that dignity within their created servitude. | terra: God honors the children of Adam and carries/provides for them, keeping human dignity within the universal creaturely dependence described by the image.

luna: The verse says God has no ally out of ذُلٍّ; the source section's lowliness belongs to the servant, never to the sovereign who needs no helper. | terra: God has no helper arising from weakness or lowliness; the source’s owner never occupies the humiliated dependent position of a servant.
luna: The verse says Iblis was among the jinn and disobeyed his Lord's command to prostrate to Adam; it makes the honored servant scene a test of obedience to the true Lord.
terra: A servant from among God’s servants receives mercy and divinely taught knowledge, showing service alongside special honor and gift.
terra: Jesus says “I am the servant of God” while recounting the Book and prophethood given to him; divinely favored status remains abd-status.

luna: The source-section root ر ب ب appears in رَبِّى وَرَبُّكُمْ; Jesus says Allah is his Lord and theirs, then commands worship of Him. | terra: After Jesus calls himself God’s servant in 19:30, he says God is “my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him,” joining his abd-status to the proper Rabb.

luna: Every being in the heavens and earth will come to the Merciful as a servant, عَبْدًا; this is the section's explicit universal created-servant claim. | terra: Everyone in heaven and earth comes to the Merciful as an عَبْدًا, directly grounding the prose’s claim that free and enslaved people alike already belong to God.

luna: The continuation says God has counted them all; it completes the universal scope in 19:93 with every individual included. | terra: God has counted and numbered every one; this makes 19:93’s universal servanthood an individually held, not merely collective, relation.

luna: The next ayah says each will come to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection; it completes the universal servant scene with individual accountability. | terra: Each will come to Him alone, completing 19:93’s scene of every creature arriving as a servant.

luna: The source-section root ع ب د appears in فَاعْبُدْنِى; God identifies Himself as Allah and commands direct service to Him. | terra: God speaks in the first person—there is no god but Me, so فَٱعْبُدْنِى—an especially close counterpart to the turn from “He” to “You” in 1:5.
luna: God makes the earth a resting place and lays out paths in it; this echoes the section's road made level and fit to be walked.
terra: God commands Moses to travel by night with “My servants”; the possessive transfers Israel from Pharaoh’s coerced service to God’s protection.
luna: The verse recounts God's command to the angels to prostrate to Adam and their compliance except for Iblis; it repeats the specific honor given to a created human.

luna: The source-section root م ل ك appears in لَهُ مَن فِى السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ, while ع ب د appears in عِبَادَتِهِ; even those near God belong to Him and are not too proud to worship. | terra: All in the heavens and earth belong to Him, and those near Him do not scorn His worship; proximity intensifies rather than cancels servanthood.
luna: The next ayah says those near Him glorify Him night and day without tiring; it completes their unceasing service in 21:19.
luna: The verse says that if there were other gods besides Allah, the heavens and earth would be ruined; it marks the boundary of exclusive lordship.

luna: The verse says every messenger was taught that there is no deity but God and to worship Him; it presents servitude as the shared prophetic message. | terra: Every messenger is sent with “there is no god but Me, so فَٱعْبُدُونِ,” combining the sole worshipped one with direct divine address.

luna: The verse calls the angels honored servants, عِبَادٌ مُّكْرَمُونَ; this directly joins the source section's honored, exalted muʿabbed sense to the servant who remains God's property. | terra: The angels are عِبَادٌ مُّكْرَمُونَ: their honor lies with, rather than above, service, answering the prose’s secondary honored sense.
luna: The continuation says the honored servants do not speak ahead of God and act by His command; it completes their honored status with obedience.
luna: The next ayah says their intercession is only by God's approval and they fear Him; it completes the honored servants' dependent standing.
luna: The passage warns that any one of them claiming to be a god besides Him would be repaid with Hell; this completes the boundary between honored service and being worshipped.
terra: “I am your Lord, so worship Me” (أَنَا۠ رَبُّكُمْ فَٱعْبُدُونِ) directly makes the Rabb relation the ground of worship.
terra: The righteous servants inherit the earth: divine ownership can honor servants with inheritance rather than leave them in a permanently low human status.
luna: The verse names people, animals, trees, mountains, and celestial bodies among those who prostrate to Allah; it renders universal subjection as a visible act.

luna: God says sacrificial camels are among His signs and provides them for people; this connects the owned animal to worship directed toward its true Owner. | terra: The sacrificial camels are made for people as God’s rites, then provide food for owner and needy; the source’s camel scene becomes provision under divine gift.
luna: The next ayah says their flesh and blood do not reach Allah, but piety does; it distinguishes the animal offered from the worshipper's obedient state.
terra: “The dominion that Day belongs to God; He will judge between them” states the owner-judge relation of Māliki yawmi d-dīn.
terra: God subjects what is on earth and the ship moving by His command, identifying all workable ground and transport as held under divine command.

luna: The verse names cattle's drink and many benefits; it makes the animal owner's benefit concrete as a gift from God. | terra: Cattle give drink, food, many benefits, and transport, a full animal-provision scene whose usefulness rests on God’s making it available.
luna: The next ayah says people are carried on livestock and ships, continuing the section's animal-as-mount scene.
luna: Noah tells his people to worship Allah alone and asks whether they will not be mindful of Him; this repeats the creature's answerability to its Lord.
luna: A messenger among the later people again commands worship of Allah alone, extending the same relation beyond Noah's community.
terra: Pharaoh’s people call Moses and Aaron’s people “servants to us,” displaying the same claimed human domination that the Exodus reverses.
luna: The question لِمَنِ الْأَرْضُ وَمَن فِيهَا asks who owns the earth and all within it, extending the section's possession image to creation.
luna: The answer to 23:84 is لِلَّهِ; this ayah contributes the explicit owner named by the preceding question.
luna: The source-section root ر ب ب appears in رَبُّ السَّمَاوَاتِ السَّبْعِ; the next ownership question directly joins God's lordship to the section's account of possession.
luna: This answer names Allah as Lord of the seven heavens; it completes 23:86's claim of lordship.

luna: The source-section root م ل ك appears in مَلَكُوتُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ; the question joins universal sovereignty to who can protect against Him. | terra: The question asks who holds the مَلَكُوت of everything in His hand, protects, and cannot be protected against; ownership is absolute command and shelter.
luna: The answer to 23:88 is that sovereignty belongs to Allah; this completes the question about ownership of everything.
luna: The verse denies any god alongside Allah and says each supposed god would take its own creation; it rules out competing owners.
luna: The verse names righteous male and female servants and calls for their marriage; it develops the household relation in which humans remain servants and dependents.

luna: The verse tells owners to make freedom contracts with those under their right hands and forbids forcing slave girls into prostitution; it sets concrete limits on ownership. | terra: Those whom the right hand possesses may seek a contract, and their owner must give them from “the wealth of God”; human possession is placed under God’s prior ownership.
luna: When believers are called to God's and the Messenger's judgment, they answer that they hear and obey; it voices the submissive stance named by the section's dīn.

luna: The verse names those whom the right hands possess in rules for asking permission at private household times; it places owned servants within the master's home and establishes a boundary for access. | terra: Those whom the right hand possesses ask leave at three private times, making the master’s house and its servants a lived household scene.
terra: The Criterion is sent down to God’s عَبْدِهِ, combining the servant name with a high prophetic commission.
terra: The One with dominion over heavens and earth has neither child nor partner and creates and measures every thing; ownership rules out both family-equality and shared rule.
luna: The verse says the supposed gods create nothing but are themselves created and have no power over harm, benefit, death, or life; the claimed lords are themselves dependent creatures.
terra: God asks those worshipped besides Him whether they misled “My servants”; false worship is staged as a contest over servants who already belong to God.
terra: “The dominion that Day belongs to the Merciful” gives the Day-of-dīn ownership claim with the very divine name under which all come as servants in 19:93.
luna: When told to prostrate to the Merciful, the deniers ask who the Merciful is and turn away; their pride reverses the servant's willing submission.

luna: The servants of the Merciful are described as walking humbly on earth; it gives a lived posture to the section's account of worship as expressed lowliness. | terra: The servants of the Merciful walk humbly on the earth; their hawn makes the section’s displayed lowliness a lived servantly bearing.

luna: Pharaoh says أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًا, claiming to have raised Moses in his household; the source-section's root ر ب ب includes this human act of nurture and mastery. | terra: Pharaoh’s “did we not raise you among us as a child?” supplies the household-master claim to which Moses answers with enslavement in 26:22.

luna: The source-section's verb عَبَّدْتَ is spoken of Pharaoh's making the Israelites slaves; it is the clearest Qur'anic human enslavement scene named by the section. | terra: Moses calls Pharaoh’s supposed favor the fact that he عَبَّدتَّ the Children of Israel, the Qur’anic human counterpart to the prose’s forced abbadta al-qawma.

luna: The verse says Pharaoh made a group of the people weak, يَسْتَضْعِفُ طَائِفَةً مِّنْهُمْ, and killed their sons while sparing their women; it expands the coercive human domination recalled in 26:22. | terra: Pharaoh exalts himself, divides the people, and weakens one group; this is dominion exercised as human abasement rather than the just lordship of God.
luna: Abraham calls his people to worship Allah and fear Him; the verse connects service to the Lord with accountability.

luna: Abraham says the idols worshipped besides Allah cannot provide sustenance, then tells the people to worship Allah and thank Him; false objects lack the provider's ownership. | terra: Those worshipped besides God cannot control provision; the verse redirects the seeker to God for provision, worship, and thanks, undoing false ownership.
terra: God addresses “My believing servants” (عِبَادِي) and says “Me alone worship”; possession by Him and the direct answer of worship stand in one sentence.

luna: Whoever is in the heavens and earth belongs to Allah, and all are قَانِتُونَ to Him; the verse directly joins universal possession to obedient service. | terra: Whoever is in heaven and earth belongs to Him and all are qānitūn, extending 19:93’s universal servant status into continual obedientness.

luna: The verse asks whether people make their owned dependents equal partners in their provision; it uses household ownership to mark the boundary between God's sovereignty and human property. | terra: The parable asks whether people would accept slaves from what their right hands possess as equal partners in their provision; it makes the owner-slave asymmetry argue against partners for God.
terra: Face the upright dīn according to God’s originating fitrah; it links true allegiance to the way God constituted humanity.
terra: God subjects what is in the heavens and earth and lavishes visible and hidden favors, broadening the tamed creature to a fitted world.

luna: The source-section root م ل ك appears in لَا يَمْلِكُونَ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ; the beings invoked besides God have no real property or share, despite being treated as lords. | terra: Claimed partners cannot possess even an atom in heaven or earth; the verse negates every rival claimant to the owner’s share.
terra: God asks the angels whether these people had worshipped them, exposing a proposed transfer of worship to a creature.
terra: The angels answer that most had worshipped jinn, not them; this identifies the actual rival service questioned in 34:40.
terra: Those called besides God do not own even a qitmir, a concrete smallest-possession boundary against treating any rival as malik.
terra: The powerless called beings cannot answer and will deny the association on the Day; it completes 35:13’s claim that they own nothing.

luna: Humankind is فقيرٌ إِلَى اللَّهِ while Allah is rich and praised; the master-servant relation is asymmetrical because every human needs God. | terra: People are needy toward God while He is the Self-Sufficient, Praised; this makes divine lordship unlike possession that depends on its servants.
terra: The believer asks why he should not worship the One who originated him and to whom he returns, making creation and return the grounds of worship.

luna: The covenant to Adam's children says not to worship Satan; it names a false master and rejects his claim to service. | terra: God’s covenant forbids worshipping Satan, an enemy master, setting a rival obedience relation against the service owed to God.

luna: The next ayah says to worship Allah, the straight path; it completes the contrast in 36:60 with the rightful object of service. | terra: “Worship Me” follows 36:60 and calls it a straight way, giving the positive master-servant response after the rejected service of Satan.

luna: The source-section root م ل ك appears in فَهُمْ لَهَا مَالِكُونَ: people own livestock, the same human master and animal-property scene developed in the section. | terra: God creates cattle “for them” and they become مَٰلِكُونَ of them, directly conjoining creaturely provision, ownership, and herd.

luna: The source-section's humbling/taming image is explicit in ذَلَّلْنَاهَا لَهُمْ; the animals are subdued for riding and other uses. | terra: وَذَلَّلْنَٰهَا uses the very tamed/subdued action developed through muzallal: people ride and eat the cattle.
terra: The same tamed herd yields benefits and drink; its final question about gratitude gives the owner’s provision the response the image requires.
terra: Everything’s مَلَكُوت is in God’s hand and all return to Him, extending hand-held ownership to the creature’s final destination.
terra: The question whether the dead will be madīnūn invokes being brought under reckoning, carrying dīn from present obedience into its final consequence.
luna: God announces that He is creating a human from clay; this neighbor supplies the created-servant context for the following prostration command.
luna: After fashioning the human and breathing into him of His spirit, God commands the angels to prostrate; this directly depicts honor bestowed by the Owner.
luna: The angels all prostrate, completing the commanded honoring of the human.
luna: Iblis alone is arrogant and refuses; this completes the passage by contrasting servitude with pride.
luna: God asks what prevented Iblis from prostrating, and Iblis claims he is better than the human; this states the prideful reversal explicitly.

luna: The source-section roots ع ب د and د ي ن meet in فَاعْبُدِ اللَّهَ and الدِّينَ; the verse commands worship with religion made pure for Him. | terra: “Worship God, making the دِين sincere for Him” joins the two named roots as exclusive allegiance.

luna: The source-section root د ي ن appears in الدِّينُ الْخَالِصُ; the verse recounts people claiming to worship intermediaries only to bring them nearer, exposing a false account of who receives service. | terra: “The pure دِين belongs to God” presents dīn as an allegiance whose rightful owner is God.

luna: The source-section root ع ب د appears in أَنْ أَعْبُدَ اللَّهَ; the speaker says he is commanded to worship Allah with sincere religion, making the worshipper's obedience explicit. | terra: The Prophet is commanded to worship God while making the dīn sincere for Him, keeping worship and dīn together in a speaking servant’s obedience.

luna: The source-section root ع ب د appears in أَعْبُدُ اللَّهَ; the speaker declares that he worships Allah with sincere religion, a first-person counterpart to 'You alone we serve.' | terra: “God I worship, making my dīn sincere for Him” gives the worshipper’s explicit first-person acceptance of that allegiance.
terra: Those who avoid worshipping tāghūt and turn to God refuse a competing master and receive the good news of that return.
luna: The source-section roots ع ب د and م ل ك meet in the parable of a slave owned by quarreling partners versus one wholly belonging to one man; it makes divided and exclusive mastery visible.
terra: God is sufficient for His servant; the master’s sufficiency answers the dependent servant’s need for help in 1:5.
terra: God directly calls the transgressing “My servants” and opens mercy to them; possession by the Lord includes care rather than abandonment.
terra: The keys of the heavens and earth belong to God, rendering His ownership through the concrete possession of access and stores.
luna: On Judgment Day the whole earth is in God's grasp and the heavens are folded in His right; the image makes every human holding subordinate to the Owner.
terra: “Call upon God, making the dīn sincere for Him” binds dīn to exclusive directed devotion under God’s authority.

luna: The source-section root م ل ك appears in لِمَنِ الْمُلْكُ الْيَوْمَ; the answer is لِلَّهِ الْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ, exposing all human ownership as subordinate on Judgment Day. | terra: Its question “to whom belongs the dominion today?” answers with the One, the Compeller, making the Day of dīn a day on which ownership is undivided.

luna: God commands people to call upon Him and says those too proud for His worship enter Hell humbled; refusal of service ends in the very abasement the image describes. | terra: Those too proud for “My worship” will enter humiliated; refusal of the servant posture turns into the very abasement the image associates with subjection.

luna: God makes livestock for people, including mounts and food; this gives the owned-animal scene the prior relation of divine provision. | terra: God made cattle so that people ride some and eat some, repeating the bodily uses of the subdued herd.

luna: The continuation says people ride the animals and reach needs they could not otherwise reach; it completes 40:79's account of livestock as provision. | terra: Their further benefits carry people to destinations; this extends 40:79’s ride-and-food scene to transport and travel.
terra: Sun and moon are not to be prostrated to; worship belongs to their Creator, who owns the objects people might otherwise elevate.
terra: God is gentle with His servants and provides for whom He wills, rendering the owner’s care and provision without reducing Him to a human master.
terra: Alleged partners legislate a dīn God did not permit, showing rival authorities attempting to claim the master’s right to prescribe obedience.
terra: The dominion of heavens and earth belongs to God, who creates and apportions children, linking ownership to origination and gift.
luna: The earth is made a resting place with routes in it; this is a second direct formulation of the road and prepared-ground image.

luna: The verse introduces the ships and livestock made for riding; 43:13 supplies the cited row's distinct point that God subdued them and the riders remember Him. | terra: The Creator made ships and cattle for people to ride; 43:13 turns that created utility into praise of the One who subjected it.

luna: The riding animal is described as سَخَّرَ لَنَا هَٰذَا, then the rider is told to remember the Lord's favor and return to Him; subduing leads into gratitude and accountability. | terra: On the backs of ships and animals people remember the One who subjected them for us, making riding an acknowledgment that human control was given.
luna: The ride's closing words say إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا لَمُنقَلِبُونَ; this neighbour completes the passage by making travel on a subdued mount point toward return to the Lord.

luna: The source-section root ع ب د appears in عِبَادُ الرَّحْمَٰنِ; the verse calls angels servants of the Merciful while rejecting their being assigned as daughters. | terra: The angels are servants of the Merciful, yet people make them female; the verse rejects recasting servants as divine offspring.
luna: The verse says God raised some people above others in ranks so that they take one another into service, سُخْرِيًّا; this directly develops human subordination and labor.
terra: Pharaoh makes his people light and they obey him, a compact portrait of a ruler manufacturing the submission the image distinguishes from worship of God.
terra: Jesus is only a servant upon whom God bestowed favor, a direct correction of elevating a favored servant into a lord.

luna: Jesus says Allah is his Lord and the people's Lord, then commands worship of Him; the creature serves the Lord without becoming one. | terra: Jesus says God is “my Rabb and your Rabb, so worship Him,” joining shared Lordship and worship in the same address.
terra: Moses tells Pharaoh to hand over “the servants of God” (عِبَادَ ٱللَّهِ), directly opposing Pharaoh’s claim over Israel to their divine belonging.
terra: Everything in the heavens and earth is subjected from Him, the comprehensive form of the animal and ground made usable for people.
terra: The one who takes his own desire as his god turns an inner appetite into the object of service, a reversal of the servant’s allegiance to God.
luna: After battle, captives are to be released or ransomed when the fighting ends; this gives a specific boundary to the human-captive scene.

luna: The source-section root ع ب د appears in لِيَعْبُدُونِ; God says He created jinn and humans only to worship Him, stating why created beings belong in the servant role. | terra: لِيَعْبُدُونِ joins createdness to worship, the precise relation behind being God’s abd by origination.
terra: God neither wants provision from His worshippers nor food; the master does not depend on what His servants supply.
terra: The dying are challenged: if you are not مَدِينِينَ, subject to authority or requital, why cannot you reverse death in 56:87?
terra: “Bring it back, if you are truthful” supplies the powerless human test that exposes the claim of being outside dīn in 56:86.

luna: The source-section root م ل ك appears in لَهُ الْمُلْكُ; dominion of the heavens and earth belongs to Him, and He gives life and death, extending the malik image to all existence. | terra: His is the dominion; He gives life and death, so the master’s possession governs the servants’ existence rather than merely their goods.
luna: The verse tells people to spend from what God has made them successors over; human possession is a trust received from the true Owner.
luna: The expiation for a husband's retraction of a declaration of separation includes freeing a slave before the spouses resume relations; it reverses ownership through release.
terra: Blessed is the One in whose hand is ٱلْمُلْك and who is powerful over every thing, a direct account of Mālik as effective possession.

luna: The source-section dictionary form مُذَلَّل (made tame) meets the earth made ذَلُولًا: people walk on its shoulders and eat its provision, while the verse ends by naming resurrection and return. | terra: God makes the earth ذَلُولًا: people walk its paths and eat His provision, extending the tamed road image to the inhabited ground itself.

luna: The earth is spread out as a carpet; this parallels the section's level, trodden ground. | terra: God makes the earth a spread surface for people, a ground prepared for the traversable road described in the image.

luna: The next verse says people may travel its broad routes; it completes 71:19 with the walked path that the source-section's road image specifies. | terra: It gives the purpose of the spread earth: people travel its wide paths, completing 71:19’s made-fit ground.
terra: The messenger says he does not possess for people either harm or right guidance, marking a human’s limit beneath the owner who can provide both.
terra: God’s servants drink from a spring they make flow abundantly, a provision scene in which the servant is received and supplied.
luna: The righteous give food to a needy person, an orphan, and a captive, أَسِيرًا; the captive is treated as a human dependent rather than merely held property.
terra: Paradise’s fruit clusters are made low and accessible, applying tadhlīl to provision rather than to an animal or person.
terra: Pharaoh’s “I am your highest Lord” (رَبُّكُمُ ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ) is the tyrant’s false claim to the Rabb-role that belongs to God alone.

luna: The source-section root د ي ن also names the Day of Recompense; this ayah asks what will make one know that day. | terra: It names يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ; 82:19 then specifies its decisive loss of all creaturely possession.

luna: The verse repeats the question about the Day of Recompense, reinforcing the source-section's second sense of dīn before the passage defines its consequence. | terra: The repeated question intensifies the Day of dīn before 82:19 defines it as God’s day of sole command.

luna: On that day no soul has power to help another and command belongs to Allah; this completes the dīn passage with the servant's helplessness before the sole Owner. | terra: On يَوْمَ ٱلدِّينِ no soul “possesses” (تَمْلِكُ) anything for another and the command belongs wholly to God, an exact expansion of 1:4.
luna: The source section's secondary dictionary sense links muʿabbed with honor; here a person reads increased provision as being honored by his Lord, a claim the passage immediately tests.
luna: The same passage contrasts reduced provision, which the person reads as humiliation; it exposes the human status reversal alongside the section's master-servant image.
luna: The correction says the people fail to honor the orphan; this turns the passage's honor language toward how humans treat those with less power.
terra: The satisfied soul is invited to enter “among My servants” (عِبَادِي), portraying final acceptance and honor inside belonging to God.

luna: The verse names freeing a neck, فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ, as the steep path; it turns the slave image into a concrete act of liberation. | terra: Releasing a neck is named as ascent on the steep way, reversing the enslaving and lowering side of the image.
luna: The next ayah adds feeding on a day of hunger; it continues the same path of releasing and sustaining people in need.
terra: The rebuke targets one who forbids a servant when he prays, staging human interference with the servant’s direct worship of his true master.
terra: “Prostrate and draw near” supplies the commanded worshipful answer to the obstruction described in 96:10.

luna: The source-section roots ع ب د and د ي ن meet in لِيَعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ الدِّينَ, explicitly joining worship and religion. | terra: People are commanded only to worship God, sincere to Him in the دِين; the verse recasts the image’s obedience as an exclusive religious act.
luna: The source-section's root ر ب ب appears in فَلْيَعْبُدُوا رَبَّ هَٰذَا الْبَيْتِ: the Lord of the House is the one to be worshipped, bringing household ownership into divine service.
luna: The next ayah says this Lord feeds against hunger and secures against fear, completing the call to worship the Lord of the House with His care for dependents.
terra: Denying the dīn opens the passage whose person repels the orphan and withholds food, setting refusal of final accountability against responsibility for those without power.
terra: “I do not worship what you worship” marks a concrete refusal to give the act of service to another claimed object of worship.
terra: “You are not worshippers of what I worship” identifies the opposing service relation in the exchange.
terra: “Your dīn for you and my dīn for me” names the separated allegiances after the reciprocal refusals of worship.
terra: رَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ names God as the people’s Lord; with 114:2–3 it restates the section’s Lord-owner-worshipped triad.
terra: مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ gives the people’s Lord the explicit owner-king role; 114:1 and 114:3 supply Rabb and Ilāh beside it.
terra: إِلَٰهِ ٱلنَّاسِ completes 114:1–3: the one who is Lord and King is also the one worshipped.
